Nadia had promised herself she would not cry at the regional science fair, but when the judge walked past her table without stopping, her throat tightened anyway.

Her project was a water filter constructed from sand, gravel, and activated charcoal packed into a carefully cut plastic bottle. It was not especially impressive to look at. Across the aisle, a boy named Theo had built a robotic arm that poured lemonade into paper cups, and an enthusiastic crowd of parents had gathered around it, laughing and applauding every time another cup filled.

Nadia looked down at her own table, where two jars sat side by side: one full of cloudy brown pond water, the other nearly transparent. She had spent three entire weekends testing different combinations of layers, recording every result in a notebook whose corners had grown soft from constant handling.

"Is this the one that cleans water?"

She looked up to see a girl of about seven standing at the edge of the table, holding her grandmother's hand and pointing at the clear jar as if it were a magic trick.

"It doesn't make it safe to drink," Nadia explained quickly. "But it removes most of the dirt, because the sand catches the larger particles and the charcoal traps substances you can't even see."

The girl's grandmother leaned closer. "Where we lived before, we had to boil everything, every pot, every single morning," she said quietly. "Does a filter like this cost very much?"

"Almost nothing," Nadia replied. "You only need a bottle and some inexpensive materials from a garden store."

The grandmother nodded thoughtfully and asked if she could copy the diagram. Nadia tore a clean page from the back of her notebook and drew it again, labeling each layer with careful, deliberate handwriting.

When the judges announced the winners an hour later, Nadia's name was not called, but she applauded for Theo anyway. In her pocket, folded small, was the thank-you note the little girl had drawn for her: a bottle, a jar of clear water, and a lopsided, smiling sun.
stem: Which statement best expresses a theme of the passage?
choices: Winning an award is the only true measure of a good project.
The worth of our work can lie in how it helps others.
Flashy inventions are usually more useful than simple ones.
Younger children often understand science better than adults.
explanation: Nadia does not win, yet the grandmother copies her diagram and the girl gives her a thank-you note, showing her project mattered in a real way.

The summer I turned twelve, my father decided I was finally old enough to work in his hardware store on Saturday mornings. I imagined myself operating the cash register with the confidence of a bank teller. Instead, he handed me a broom and pointed toward the storage room, where thirty years of sawdust had settled into every corner and crevice.

For the entire first month, I swept. I sorted loose screws into tiny drawers labeled in my father's cramped handwriting, and I discovered that a wood screw and a machine screw look nearly identical until you examine them side by side. I was thoroughly bored, and I made certain that everyone around me knew it.

Then one Saturday in July, an elderly customer arrived holding a broken faucet handle. Because my father was occupied with a delivery, the man turned hopefully to me. I panicked, since I had no idea what the part was called, let alone where to locate it.

But as I turned the handle over in my hands, something clicked. I had sorted a hundred parts exactly like it. I walked confidently to the third aisle, pulled open the drawer second from the bottom, and found a perfect match. The man tested it right there at the counter, and it fit precisely.

"Your father certainly trained you well," he remarked.

I wanted to explain that my father hadn't trained me at all, that I had only been sweeping and sorting. Then I realized that the sweeping and sorting had been exactly the training. Every tedious drawer had been a lesson I didn't know I was taking.

My father never admitted that he had planned it that way, and I never asked him. But the following Saturday, when he handed me the broom, I accepted it without complaining.
stem: What is the central idea of this memoir?
choices: Children should not be asked to work in a family business.
Simple, dull tasks can teach skills we don't notice learning.
Customers trust older workers more than younger ones.
A good store must keep its parts sorted in labeled drawers.
explanation: The narrator realizes that the sweeping and sorting "had been exactly the training" and that every tedious drawer "had been a lesson I didn't know I was taking."

passage:
Every autumn, forests across much of North America turn from green to brilliant shades of red, orange, and gold. Many people assume the leaves are changing into new colors. In fact, many of those colors were present all along.

During spring and summer, leaves are packed with chlorophyll, a green pigment that plants use to capture energy from sunlight. Chlorophyll is so plentiful that it hides the other pigments in the leaf, much as a bright spotlight can wash out the glow of a candle. Among these hidden pigments are carotenoids, which produce yellow and orange. Carotenoids are the same substances that give carrots and corn their color.

As days grow shorter and nights grow cooler, trees prepare for winter. Many trees cannot keep their broad, thin leaves alive through freezing weather, so they begin to shut down food production. The tree stops making new chlorophyll, and the green pigment that remains breaks down. As the green fades, the yellows and oranges finally show through.

Reds and purples work differently. These colors come from pigments called anthocyanins, which many trees produce only in the fall. Scientists believe anthocyanins may act like a sunscreen, protecting the leaf while the tree pulls valuable nutrients out of it before it drops. Sunny days and cool nights tend to produce the most anthocyanins, which is why some autumns are far more colorful than others.

Eventually, a layer of cells forms where the leaf stem meets the branch. This layer slowly cuts the leaf off from the tree, and the leaf falls. The tree, now bare, will rest until spring, when the cycle begins again.
stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Fall colors appear as leaf pigments change while trees prepare for winter.
Carrots and corn get their color from the same pigments as fall leaves.
Trees lose their leaves because freezing weather damages their branches.
Scientists still do not know why leaves change color in the autumn.
explanation: The passage explains how chlorophyll breaks down to reveal yellows and oranges and how anthocyanins add reds as trees get ready for winter.

passage:
In the early 1800s, moving goods across New York State was slow and costly. Roads were rough dirt tracks that turned to mud in the rain, and a wagon loaded with grain might take weeks to travel from the Great Lakes to the Atlantic coast. Farmers in the western part of the state often found it cheaper to send their crops south than to ship them east.

Governor DeWitt Clinton believed the answer was a canal: a human-made waterway stretching more than 360 miles from Albany, on the Hudson River, to Buffalo, on Lake Erie. Many people thought the plan was foolish. Critics mocked it as "Clinton's Ditch," and even President Thomas Jefferson reportedly called it "little short of madness."

Construction began in 1817. Workers, many of them recent immigrants, dug the channel largely by hand, using shovels, horses, and simple machines. Engineers had little formal training, so they learned as they went. To carry boats over hills and valleys, they built a series of locks, which are chambers that raise or lower boats by filling or draining water.

When the canal opened in 1825, the doubters were quickly proven wrong. Mule-drawn boats could now carry goods from Buffalo to New York City in a fraction of the time, and shipping costs dropped dramatically. Towns such as Rochester and Syracuse grew rapidly along the canal's banks. New York City became the busiest port in the nation, and settlers poured into the Midwest, knowing their crops could reach eastern markets.

Within a few decades, railroads began to replace canals as the fastest way to move freight. Yet the Erie Canal had already done its work. It had shown that a bold public project could reshape the economy of an entire region.

choices: Railroads were a better invention than canals in the 1800s.
Building a canal by hand was dangerous work for immigrants.

DeWitt Clinton was the most popular governor in New York history.
explanation: The passage describes the doubts about the canal and then shows how it cut shipping costs, grew towns, and made New York City the busiest port.

Winter Orchard

The orchard holds its breath in February,
each branch a dark sentence left unfinished,
written in a hand the frost keeps correcting,
while snow has filed the hills down to a whisper.

My grandfather walked these rows for fifty years,
pruning with the deliberate patience of a man
who trusted what he could not see:
the sap asleep inside the bark like ink
inside a capped pen, waiting.

Now the ladders lean against the empty shed,
their rungs gone silver with disuse,
and crows convene on the fence posts
like a council that has misplaced its agenda.

Still, I have learned to read the bark:
beneath each knot, a bud is clenched
as tightly as a fist around a coin,
and the coin is April.

So I walk the rows the way he walked them,
not to harvest anything,
but to keep the promise the trees are keeping,
to stand in the cold and believe in green.

explanation: The speaker walks the rows "the way he walked them" to "believe in green," echoing the grandfather who "trusted what he could not see."

In an age of disposable goods, the ability to fix things has quietly vanished from many households. When a toaster stops working or a chair wobbles, the most common response is not to open it up but to throw it away and order a replacement. Schools, which once routinely offered shop classes and home economics, have largely abandoned instruction in practical repair. This is a mistake, and it is one that schools should correct by making basic repair skills part of the standard curriculum.

The first argument for teaching repair is economic. Replacing an appliance often costs many times more than replacing the small part that failed. A student who can diagnose a broken hinge or a frayed cord gains a skill that will save money for the rest of his or her life, a lesson in financial independence more concrete than any worksheet on budgeting.

The second argument is environmental. Discarded electronics and furniture accumulate in landfills at an alarming rate, and the manufacture of each replacement consumes energy and raw materials. Every object that is repaired rather than replaced represents a small reduction in waste. Multiplied across millions of households, those small reductions become significant.

Critics contend that the school day is already crowded and that time spent on repair would come at the expense of academic subjects. This objection, however, rests on a false distinction. Repairing a device requires reading technical diagrams, forming and testing hypotheses, and applying principles of physics and geometry. Far from distracting students from academic learning, repair puts that learning to work in a setting where mistakes have visible consequences and success is immediately apparent.

Finally, repair cultivates a disposition that extends beyond any single object: the conviction that problems can be understood and solved through patient investigation. Students who learn that a silent radio can be coaxed back to life may approach other challenges, whether in science, in their communities, or in their own lives, with the same confidence.

The objects around us were designed by people, and they can be understood by people. Schools should ensure that every graduate leaves knowing it.

On a summer afternoon, the downtown core of a large city can be several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside, and after sunset the difference may grow even larger. Climate scientists call this phenomenon the urban heat island effect, and as cities expand and summers intensify, understanding it has become a matter of public health.

The effect arises primarily from the materials cities are built with. Asphalt, concrete, and dark roofing absorb a large fraction of incoming sunlight and store it as heat. Whereas vegetation releases moisture through its leaves, a process called evapotranspiration that cools the surrounding air much as perspiration cools the skin, paved surfaces offer no such relief. Tall buildings compound the problem by trapping warm air in narrow streets and by blocking breezes that would otherwise disperse it. Heat generated by vehicles, air conditioners, and industry adds still more.

Perhaps counterintuitively, the heat island is often most pronounced at night. Throughout the day, dense urban materials accumulate thermal energy; after dark, they release it slowly, keeping city temperatures elevated long after rural areas have cooled. This nighttime warmth carries real consequences. The human body depends on cooler nighttime temperatures to recover from daytime heat, and during prolonged heat waves, the absence of that relief contributes to heat-related illness, particularly among elderly residents and those without air conditioning.

Fortunately, the factors that create heat islands also suggest remedies. Cities on several continents have experimented with "cool roofs," coated with reflective materials that bounce sunlight back into the sky rather than absorbing it. Others have expanded tree canopies, converted vacant lots into parks, and replaced conventional pavement with lighter or more porous alternatives. Researchers caution that no single strategy is sufficient; the most effective approaches combine several interventions and prioritize the neighborhoods where residents are most vulnerable.

The urban heat island is, in a sense, a problem of design. Because people built the conditions that produce it, people can also rebuild them.

You asked in your last letter whether I regret coming west, and I confess I have delayed my reply because I wished to answer honestly rather than merely cheerfully. The schoolhouse is constructed of sod, which is to say of the prairie itself, cut into rectangular blocks and stacked like bricks. I have nineteen scholars enrolled, though rarely all of them at once. During planting and harvest the older boys are required in the fields, and I cannot in good conscience scold them for their absence, since their families' survival depends upon the crop considerably more than upon the multiplication tables. Several of the children speak German or Norwegian at home and are acquiring English alongside their arithmetic. Last week little Anna Halvorsen read an entire page aloud without assistance, and her mother, who had come to fetch her, wept openly at the door; I own that I did as well.

Loneliness is the most difficult trial of this existence. The nearest neighbor lives two miles distant, and in the evenings the wind across the grass produces a sound so continuous that one ceases to hear it until it stops, whereupon the silence becomes nearly unbearable. I reread your letters until the folds wear through.

And yet, dear Margaret, I do not regret my decision. In Ohio I was merely one teacher among many, and I occasionally wondered whether my absence would be noticed at all. Here, if I do not open the door in the morning, there is simply no school. I have never before been so exhausted, nor so entirely certain that my labor mattered.

Your loving sister,
Clara
